word:lxx:L700241.explanation: This word is a proper name rendered “Addō” or “Aththo.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times across six verses, in 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Zechariah. The name occurs in passages associated with different individuals named Addō, so the surrounding verse is needed to identify which person is intended. Its basic function remains that of a personal name.

word:lxx:L700296.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “impossible”: it describes something that cannot be done, achieved, or brought about. As a verb, it expresses inability rather than naming a person or object. It appears 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of statements. Its first listed occurrence is Genesis 18:14, and its final occurrence is Wisdom 13:16; the precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L700313.explanation: Aenaos means ever-flowing, describing a flow that continues without stopping.

word:lxx:L700450.explanation: This verb describes becoming numb or losing normal sensation, expressed by the meanings “become dumb” and “become tingly.” It refers to a change in bodily feeling or ability, rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs twice, both times in Jeremiah 38:29–30. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is becoming numb or becoming unable to speak.

word:lxx:L700502.explanation: This word means “captive”—a person taken and held by others, unable to live freely. It functions as a noun or adjective, identifying someone who has been captured or is in captivity. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, in Genesis 31:26 and Exodus 12:29. Its basic meaning remains focused on a person’s condition as one held captive, while the surrounding verse determines the specific circumstances.

word:lxx:L700656.explanation: Aletheia means truth. Truth is described as established in the heavens, and people can act in truth and integrity.

word:lxx:L700681.explanation: This noun means “change,” referring to an alteration from one state, condition, or arrangement to another. It names the fact or process of things becoming different, rather than describing a person or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in the Wisdom of Solomon. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a change or alteration.

word:lxx:L700739.explanation: Alōēs; Alis is a proper name belonging to a person mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. As a name, it identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or general idea. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Nehemiah 10:25. The available information establishes the name and its use as a personal designation, but it does not provide the surrounding verse text or enough context to explain anything further about the person. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on reading the surrounding context.

word:lxx:L700775.explanation: Hamartia means sin. It can also refer to a fault.

word:lxx:L700818.explanation: This word means “amen”: an interjection used as a brief, affirmative response. It expresses agreement with, or confirmation of, what has been said, prayed, or proclaimed. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs five times—three times in Old Testament books and twice in deuterocanonical books. Its repeated rendering as “Amen” preserves the same concise expression rather than translating it into a longer phrase.

word:lxx:L700821.explanation: This adjective describes something kept clean, pure, and free from defilement—“untainted” or “undefiled.” It can describe a person or condition regarded as unpolluted rather than corrupted. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs five times, all in Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. The English rendering “undefiled” appears in each recorded occurrence, reinforcing the word’s consistent sense of moral or ritual purity. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L700854.explanation: This noun means “forgetfulness of wrong: an amnesty.” It refers to setting aside an offense so that the wrong is no longer held against someone. In ordinary terms, it describes pardon expressed as abandoning a grievance, rather than simply failing to remember an ordinary fact. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in the book of Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording.

word:lxx:L700933.explanation: Anagō means to lead up or bring up.

word:lxx:L700995.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “slip away”: to leave, depart, or move out of reach. It describes withdrawal or passing away rather than remaining in place. The word occurs 14 times in the deuterocanonical Greek writings represented here, appearing in Wisdom, Sirach, and 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or who is departing and on the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L701022.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “bringing up” or “raising up.” It describes the act of lifting, bringing something forward, or causing it to rise. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at Genesis 50:24. Its basic meaning remains broad because the surrounding verse text is not included, so the precise object or action must be understood from that passage. As a noun, it names the act or process itself rather than functioning as a command or description of a person.

word:lxx:L701220.explanation: This Greek Old Testament noun means “answer”—a reply given in response to a question, challenge, or statement. It presents the idea of responding rather than speaking without a prompt. In the Septuagint, it occurs twice, both times in Job, showing a focused use rather than a broadly repeated term. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and conversation, but its central meaning remains a spoken or expressed reply.

word:lxx:L701314.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as “sung of; famous in song.” It points to a subject remembered or celebrated through singing, especially as worthy of being made known in song. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, at 4 Maccabees 10:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is fame expressed through song or poetic praise.

word:lxx:L701358.explanation: Apartia means baggage, or what is moved.

word:lxx:L701361.explanation: This verb means “offer” or “begin.” It can describe presenting something, especially as an offering, or starting an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, concentrated mainly in 2 Chronicles, with one occurrence in Proverbs. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on what action or object accompanies it, but its normal range is straightforward: to offer something or to begin doing something.

word:lxx:L701426.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “step off” or “step away.” It describes moving away from a place or position, with the surrounding sentence determining the specific situation. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages from Exodus, Job, Proverbs, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. It is especially frequent in Job, where it appears 15 times. Its basic idea remains physical or figurative departure from a point of standing or activity.

word:lxx:L701484.explanation: This verb means “shut up”: to close something or keep it from being open or accessible. It describes an action of blocking or enclosing, rather than merely stopping speech. In the Greek LXX, it occurs 27 times across the Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing repeated use for closing or restricting access in different passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being closed or confined there.

word:lxx:L701677.explanation: Arad, also rendered Arath, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named biblical entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs eight times in the LXX, appearing in Genesis, Numbers, and Judges. Because the supplied lexical information gives the name but not a fuller definition or the identity of the person or place named, its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding passage. The form is rendered “Arad” in the available translation evidence.

word:lxx:L701743.explanation: This adjective means “easily numbered” or “few in number.” It describes something limited enough to be counted readily, emphasizing its small or manageable total rather than a particular quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Job, so its normal use is narrowly attested within the LXX corpus. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being counted, but the word itself points to something readily countable or few.

word:lxx:L702030.explanation: This noun means “inviolability”: the condition of being protected from violation. It describes a status that others are expected to respect, rather than an action someone performs. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:12. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise force there cannot be described further; its established lexical sense is the protected, inviolable status itself.

word:lxx:L702236.explanation: Aphrōn means senseless, describing a foolish person.

word:lxx:L702373.explanation: This word is a proper name rendered “Batharōth” or “Vatharoth.” It identifies a named place in the Greek Old Testament wording of Joshua 19:6. Because it appears only once in the LXX corpus, its meaning is limited to this geographic name rather than a general idea, action, or quality. The two renderings are name variants, not separate concepts within this usage.

word:lxx:L702399.explanation: Baitharan, also rendered Vetharan, is a proper name rather than a descriptive word. It identifies a named person, place, or other specific entity in the Greek Old Testament text; the available lexical information does not specify which kind. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 32:36. Its precise referent is therefore determined by the surrounding verse and passage, not by the name alone.

word:lxx:L702467.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered “Balaa” or “Valaa.” It identifies a particular named person, place, or other entity rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles. The available references establish its use as a name, but without the surrounding verse text they do not determine the exact referent in each occurrence. Its precise identification therefore depends on the genealogical or listing context of those passages.

word:lxx:L702562.explanation: Basaloth is a proper name, also rendered Vasaloth. It functions as a name rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears two times: once in Ezra 2:52 and once in Nehemiah 7:54. The name itself does not provide a broader ordinary meaning beyond identifying the named entity in those passages. Its exact referent is determined by the surrounding lists and context, which are not included here.

word:lxx:L702629.explanation: Bezek, also rendered Vezek, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies the named entity represented by this Greek LXX term. Within the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in Judges 1:4–5. The available lexical meaning is therefore the name itself: Bezek or Vezek. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

word:lxx:L702665.explanation: This word is a proper name: “Beselēl” or “Veselil.” It functions as a personal name rather than a general description, so its meaning is chiefly the person designated by that name. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Ezra 10:30. Without the verse text, the name itself does not provide additional information about that person’s role or the surrounding event.

word:lxx:L702760.explanation: Booz, also rendered Vooz, is a proper name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named in several books, especially Ruth, where the name appears frequently. It occurs 32 times across 28 verses in the LXX Old Testament, from Exodus to Isaiah. The name’s exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and narrative, but its basic function remains the same: it identifies the person called Booz.

word:lxx:L702812.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “shower” or “rain,” describing water falling from the sky. It can refer to ordinary rainfall or to a significant downpour, depending on the surrounding passage. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in passages from Genesis through Amos. Its central idea remains the act of rain falling, whether presented as a needed provision or as part of a powerful event. The exact force in any verse depends on its immediate context.

word:lxx:L702908.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered “Gaibenenom; Yevenenom.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general category. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 28:3. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text or a broader lexical definition, its exact identity and role must be determined from that passage’s context.

word:lxx:L702931.explanation: The word is a proper name for the Galatai, also given as Galate. It identifies a named people or group rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in 1 Maccabees 8:2 and once in 2 Maccabees 8:20. Its exact reference in either passage requires the surrounding verse text for contextual detail.

word:lxx:L702944.explanation: Gamali is a proper name referring to a person. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears once, in Numbers 13:12. As a personal name, it identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or general idea. The available wording preserves the name as “Gamali,” so its ordinary meaning here is the person’s name itself. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain that individual’s role in the passage.

word:lxx:L703037.explanation: Genea means generation. It can mark successive descent, as children are counted to a third generation, and an observance kept in every generation.

word:lxx:L703169.explanation: This word means “parent”: a father or mother viewed in relation to a child. It is a noun used for an individual parent or, in the plural, for parents together. In this LXX corpus, it occurs 12 times, including passages in Esther, Proverbs, Wisdom, and the Maccabean books. The central idea is the family relationship between a child and the father or mother identified as the parent. Its precise reference in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L703266.explanation: Dalida is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is also represented as “Thalitha” in the lexical definition. In this Greek LXX corpus, the name occurs ten times, all in Judges 16. The available references show repeated use of the name, while the surrounding verse text is not included here, so the person’s specific role must be understood from the passages themselves.

word:lxx:L703288.explanation: This noun means “money spent”—an amount used or paid out for a purpose. It points to expenditure rather than to money merely possessed, emphasizing what has been laid out in payment. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both in 2 Maccabees, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the immediate context.

word:lxx:L703392.explanation: “Dephrōna; Thefrona” is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a specific name in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once, in Numbers 34:9. The available wording identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain its precise referent or significance. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the name “Dephrōna; Thefrona,” with the passage supplying the context for whom or what it designates.

word:lxx:L703587.explanation: This noun means “standing aloof” or “separation”—being apart rather than joined together. It can describe a state of distance or withdrawal. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:7; the precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains separation: a condition in which people or things stand apart.

word:lxx:L703604.explanation: This verb means “stretch to the uttermost”: to extend something as far as it can go or to reach out fully. As a verb, it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs five times across Psalms, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being extended and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains maximum extension or reach.

word:lxx:L703648.explanation: This word means “teacher”—a person who instructs or guides others in learning. As a noun, it identifies the person rather than the act of teaching. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Esther and once in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on someone who provides instruction, while the surrounding passage determines what is being taught and how the person’s role is being presented.

word:lxx:L703671.explanation: This verb means to search through something or examine it closely. It describes an active, careful investigation rather than a quick glance. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both in the book of Wisdom. The word can therefore express the effort to look carefully into something in order to understand, inspect, or discover what is there. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being examined.

word:lxx:L703752.explanation: This noun refers to prepared hide or tanned skin—animal skin treated so it could be used as a durable material. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 39:20. The word identifies the material itself rather than an action or quality, but the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how that material is being used there. Its basic meaning remains a worked, usable skin prepared for a practical purpose.

word:lxx:L703846.explanation: This Greek LXX adverb means “strongly” or “mightily,” describing how an action is carried out. It adds the idea of power, force, or great strength to the verb it modifies, rather than naming a person or thing. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus: once in 1 Chronicles and once in Wisdom. In both places, it is rendered “mightily,” supporting the sense of acting with notable strength or power. Its exact emphasis in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L703891.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Dōdia,” also identified as “Thothia.” It is a personal designation rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 1 Chronicles 27:4 and once in 2 Chronicles 20:37. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the particular person and role in each passage must be understood from those contexts.

word:lxx:L703947.explanation: This word means “guarantee.” As an adjective, it describes someone or something that serves as a guarantee or provides assurance. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament writings represented here: twice in Sirach and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is dependable assurance—a person or thing presented as security that something will be fulfilled or upheld.

word:lxx:L704111.explanation: Eisdechomai means to receive, including someone who has been cast out.

word:lxx:L704128.explanation: This noun means “gathering in.” It refers to the act of bringing something in or collecting it, rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within Exodus 30:13–16. Its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains an act of gathering or bringing in. The word is therefore best understood as a term describing collection or intake within the passage where it appears.

word:lxx:L704164.explanation: This verb means “strip off the skin from.” It describes the physical act of removing an outer skin or hide from something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, so it is a specific action word rather than a broad term for general removal. Its exact force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains the removal of skin from an animal or other object. The word functions as a verb, expressing what someone does.

word:lxx:L704209.explanation: Ekkas is a proper name, referring to a person named Ekkas rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 2 Samuel 23:26. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide additional meaning or an explanation of the person’s role. Its significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and narrative context.

word:lxx:L704245.explanation: This verb means “lacking”—being without something needed or expected. It describes a deficiency rather than naming the person or thing that is missing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Zechariah 11:16. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise role in that passage must be understood from the larger context. Its central sense remains the condition of lacking or failing to have something.

word:lxx:L704300.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “flow out”: it describes something moving outward from a source, usually as a liquid or stream. It is a word of outward movement rather than simply existing or remaining in place. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, including passages in Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force—what is flowing and from where—depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains movement outward or away from a source.

word:lxx:L704397.explanation: Elaunō means to drive. It can also mean to row.

word:lxx:L704476.explanation: This noun means “coil”: something wound or arranged in a circular or spiral form. It names a physical shape rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at Genesis 49:11. Because the surrounding verse text is not included, the word’s precise role in that passage must be understood from its context, but its basic lexical sense remains a coil or winding shape.

word:lxx:L704498.explanation: Eliphalias, also rendered Elifalias, is a proper name referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 15:21. The name itself does not provide a broader definition or explain the person’s character; its specific significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:lxx:L704515.explanation: This proper name refers to a Hellene, meaning a Greek person or the Greek people. It identifies people associated with Hellenic identity rather than describing an action, feeling, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 13 times, including passages in Isaiah, Daniel, Joel, Zechariah, and the Maccabean books. The precise reference—whether to one person or a wider people—depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

word:lxx:L704559.explanation: The word is a proper name, appearing as “Emekraphain” or “Emekrafen.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, in Joshua 18:16. The name itself does not explain the entity’s location or role; those details must be understood from the surrounding passage in Joshua. Its spelling may appear differently in English transliteration, but both supplied forms represent this same biblical name.

word:lxx:L704685.explanation: Endeō means to bind in; it can also mean to be in need.

word:lxx:L704757.explanation: This verb means “live amongst,” describing people dwelling or carrying on life among others. It presents living within a community or shared setting rather than being separate from those around them. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:25. The word’s basic sense is therefore the act of residing among a group of people; the surrounding verse determines the specific situation in which that shared living is mentioned.

word:lxx:L704814.explanation: This adjective describes something that has water in it or is capable of holding water. It points to a water-containing quality rather than naming the water itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, showing a specific descriptive use rather than a broad range of meanings. Its exact force in any sentence depends on the thing being described, but the central idea remains something filled with, supplied with, or retaining water.

word:lxx:L704858.explanation: This verb means to become estranged—to be separated from someone or no longer share a close relationship. It describes a change in relationship rather than merely physical distance. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 12:10. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context, but its central idea is relational separation or alienation.

word:lxx:L704861.explanation: Exanaliskō means to spend entirely, using something up completely.

word:lxx:L704920.explanation: This noun means “expositor”: a person who explains or makes something understandable. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within three verses in Genesis and Proverbs. Its basic sense points to someone whose role is to give an explanation, especially when meaning is not immediately clear. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being explained in each occurrence.

word:lxx:L705167.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “overflow”: to flow over a boundary or spread beyond what can contain it. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, including passages from Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on what is said to overflow and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is movement that exceeds its limits.

word:lxx:L705260.explanation: Epispeudō means to urge on or further.

word:lxx:L705329.explanation: This word means “vocalize” or “call out”: it describes making one’s voice heard aloud, whether by uttering something or calling to others. As a verb, it focuses on the act of producing a spoken cry or audible expression, rather than on a particular message or emotion. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees 1:23 and once in 3 Maccabees 7:13. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what is being called out in each passage.

word:lxx:L705365.explanation: This word means “700,” or seven hundred. It is an adjective used to describe a quantity, number, or counted group. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 40 times, showing a recurring numerical use rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: it identifies an amount consisting of seven hundred. The surrounding noun or statement determines what is being counted, while the number itself contributes the precise quantity.

word:lxx:L705530.explanation: This noun means a “trial” or “affliction”—a difficult experience that brings distress, hardship, or testing. It refers to trouble endured by a person rather than to an action performed by someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Job, where it belongs to language describing human suffering and difficulty. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains an experience of severe trial or affliction.

word:lxx:L706290.explanation: Thoou is a proper name, referring to a person named Thoou or Thou. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in 2 Samuel 8:9–10. word:lxx:L706342.explanation: “Thyrsus” is a noun naming a thyrsus, a specific object or emblem referred to by that name. Its lexical meaning remains the named item “thyrsus,” while the passage supplies its particular significance.

word:lxx:L706412.explanation: Iamneia, also called Iamnia, is a proper name for a place. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being undergirded there, but the word itself points to providing support beneath something.

word:lxx:L713429.explanation: Phesē, also rendered Fesi, is a proper name referring to a person named in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Greek text, at Nehemiah 7:51, and its precise significance is limited to identifying that person. The available lexical information does not provide a broader meaning or word-picture beyond the personal name itself.

word:lxx:L713465.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means being “fond of money.” It describes a person whose desire or preference is directed toward wealth, emphasizing an attitude toward money rather than merely possessing it. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 10:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is clear: showing an undue or notable attachment to money.

policy.priorReviewerNotes: The lexical evidence establishes the forms Phoros/Foros but does not establish the meaning or association with tribute. The Scripture renderings support tribute context, but the primary claim lacks lexical support for that exact sense. “Associated with tribute” is also too vague to teach the meaning directly.

word:lxx:L713762.explanation: Chaseleu, also called Khaselev, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or person. It identifies a named term preserved in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. The form appears seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, with one occurrence in Zechariah and six in 1–2 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the lexical meaning supplied for the name is simply “Chaseleu” or “Khaselev.”

word:lxx:L713803.explanation: Cheleg, also rendered Kheleg, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person and appears once, in Numbers 26:34. Because it is a personal name, its meaning here is chiefly identification: it distinguishes one individual from others named in the surrounding genealogical record. The name itself does not provide a general teaching or concept apart from the person it names.

word:lxx:L713982.explanation: Chrōma means skin, as in the skin of the face.

word:lxx:L714002.explanation: This verb means to embank with earthen mounds—to build up earth into raised defenses or barriers. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 11:13. The word’s basic sense is therefore specific and practical: forming protective earthworks around or near a place. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how that action functions there.
